text:
Walking to School

Twenty years ago, most children in Europe walked or cycled to school. Today, in many countries, fewer than half of them do. Parents drive their children because they worry about traffic — and by driving, they make the traffic worse. Researchers call this a vicious circle: the more parents drive, the more dangerous the roads outside schools become, and the more parents decide to drive.

Some towns have tried to break the circle. In one Swiss village, the school moved the drop-off point four hundred metres away from the gate. Parents may still drive, but the last part of the journey has to be walked. Within a year, the number of cars in front of the school had fallen by two thirds, and teachers reported that the children arrived calmer than before.

Walking has other effects that are easy to overlook. Children who walk to school know their neighbourhood better; they can describe where the bakery is, which street is steep, where the water runs after heavy rain. They also arrive more awake. A short walk in daylight helps the body to understand that the day has begun — something no alarm clock can do on its own.

None of this means that every family can manage without a car. Some children live far away, some parents leave for work at six. But for the many who live within a kilometre of their school, the walk is not lost time. It is the only part of the day that belongs entirely to them.
